opus-5.5.text:
I think it's catchable, but people tend to underestimate where the hard part is.

On the surface, Operator looks like a product problem: a model that sees the screen, clicks, types, and fills forms. Many Chinese teams can build a demo like that quickly. We have strong base models now, and the vision-language capability isn't that far behind. So if you're asking whether Chinese teams can make something that looks like Operator in a few months, the answer is clearly yes.

But the real gap isn't the demo. It's reliability over long horizons. An agent that books a flight has to do maybe twenty or thirty steps correctly in a row. If each step is 95% accurate, you multiply that out and the whole task almost always fails. Getting each step from 95 to 99 percent is extremely hard, and I believe that's mostly an RL problem, not a pretraining problem.

That's where I think OpenAI's real advantage lies. First, they have the infrastructure to do large-scale reinforcement learning in real or realistic environments: thousands of browsers running in parallel, with stable rollouts, reward signals, and a way to recover when things crash. That engineering is boring but very expensive, and most teams in China haven't invested in it at that scale. People prefer to work on the model. Not many want to build the environment.

Second, there's data and feedback. Once you have a product with real users, you see how people actually use it and where it fails, and that becomes a flywheel. Without users you're guessing at the task distribution.

Third, and this is more subtle, the reasoning model matters. Operator-style agents get much better when the underlying model can plan, reflect, and notice "this didn't work, let me try something else." That ability came from the o-series style of RL training. Chinese teams are catching up quickly there. DeepSeek showed the recipe isn't secret. But combining reasoning RL with agentic, multi-turn, environment-interacting RL is still very much an open research problem.

So my overall view is that the algorithmic gap isn't huge. Maybe it's a matter of months. The gap is in systems, meaning RL infrastructure and environment engineering, and in the willingness to commit long-term resources to something that doesn't show results right away. If a Chinese team really commits to building the RL infrastructure properly, I don't think there's any fundamental barrier. The question is whether anyone has the patience to do it rather than chasing the next benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response discusses technical and infrastructure gaps, but does not mention uncertainty about OpenAI’s undisclosed progress as an obstacle to judging catch-up prospects.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that OpenAI generally releases products only after substantial internal polishing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think Operator itself is the hard part. If you look at what Operator does, it's a browser agent: it takes screenshots, reasons about the page, clicks, types, and loops. The scaffolding is not mysterious. Any decent team in China could reproduce the pipeline in a few weeks. The gap is underneath.

The first gap is the base model. An agent is only as good as the model's ability to plan over long horizons and recover from mistakes. When Operator clicks the wrong button, it notices and backtracks. That kind of robustness comes from the model, not the harness. Our open models are good at single-turn tasks, but multi-step reliability is still noticeably behind, and you only see that when you run hundreds of trajectories, not in a demo.

The second gap is data. Nobody has a lot of real browser-interaction trajectories lying around. OpenAI can collect them at scale from users and from their own labeling operations. Chinese teams have to synthesize most of it, and synthetic trajectories tend to teach the model a cleaner world than the one it will actually face. I think the teams that figure out cheap, realistic environment construction will matter more than the teams that just train bigger.

The third thing, and people underrate this, is the product environment. Chinese internet is mostly apps, not open web. Mini programs, closed ecosystems, no stable DOM. So even a perfect Operator clone would struggle here, because the surface it needs to operate on is different. That is a disadvantage for copying, but it is also an opportunity: whoever builds the agent that actually works inside WeChat or Taobao is solving a problem OpenAI isn't solving.

So my assessment is: catching up on the demo is easy, catching up on reliability is hard, and the real prize isn't catching up at all. It's building for the environment we actually have.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between reproducing a demo and building a system that people can reliably use. A demo might show an agent opening a browser, clicking through a website, and completing a task. But what happens when the page changes, a pop-up appears, or one step fails? Can it recognize the mistake and recover? That’s where the challenge becomes much harder.

For Chinese teams, I wouldn’t frame this simply as whether they can build something that looks like Operator. The question is whether they can develop the underlying capabilities and the feedback loop to keep improving reliability. That requires models, an execution environment, and good ways to evaluate whether tasks actually succeeded.

A practical approach is to start with a narrower set of tasks, make those work consistently, and then expand. There’s room to compete, especially in workflows where a team understands users very well. But catching up on a demonstration and catching up on a dependable product are two different milestones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is less about reproducing a demo and more about making the system reliable. An agent might successfully book a restaurant once, but can it handle a different website, an unexpected pop-up, or a failed payment without getting stuck? That gap is substantial.

For Chinese teams, I would look at three things: the underlying model’s ability to reason and understand interfaces, the training environments and feedback available to improve it, and the engineering needed to recover from mistakes. Those pieces have to develop together. Simply connecting a language model to a browser won’t solve the problem.

There’s also an opportunity to focus on particular tasks. You don’t necessarily have to match Operator across every website immediately. If you can make an agent consistently useful in a well-defined workflow, you can build from there. So I wouldn’t frame this as an impossible gap, but I also wouldn’t judge progress by how impressive a short demonstration looks.
